stories.headline: McKelvey and Tokuda criticize federal job cuts hitting Maui recovery
stories.summary: State Sen. Angus McKelvey and U.S. Rep. Jill Tokuda criticized federal job cuts affecting wildfire recovery, while the UH Economic Research Organization warned of more than 2,000 lost local jobs and recession risk.
stories.text: State Senator Angus McKelvey and U.S. Rep. Jill Tokuda criticized the Trump administration for federal job cuts affecting wildfire recovery efforts. Maui Economic Opportunity lost 131 jobs funded by a national dislocated worker grant, while 17 kākou Maui employees were placed on leave due to funding cuts. Senator McKelvey condemned the layoffs as a profound misstep that threatens economic stability and the well-being of our community and also praised Governor Josh Green for efforts to integrate displaced workers into state programs. He urged county governments to find solutions to keep these workers employed. The UH Economic Research Organization agrees that the clearest near-term risk is federal layoffs, which could result in a loss of more than 2,000 local jobs, fully offsetting growth in construction and the lift from local tax cuts. Together with other federal policies, this places the Hawaiʻi economy at risk of recession over the next few years. The UH The Foundation is now working to raise private donations to support graduate students that have lost their research funding and educational stipends as a result of stop work orders and freezes on federal grant funds.

stories.headline: Parking lot sleepover pilot still not implemented after two years
stories.summary: Advocates and Native Hawaiians voiced frustration at a council committee meeting that the county's approved program for homeless people to sleep in cars in parking lots has yet to start.
stories.text: More than two years after Maui County approved a pilot program allowing homeless individuals to sleep in their cars in county parking lots, it has yet to be implemented. Advocates and Native Hawaiians expressed frustration during a county council committee meeting Tuesday. Their concerns were amplified by a report linking homelessness to the 1893 U.S. overthrow of the Hawaiian Kingdom and ongoing land dispossession. Haʻikū resident Trinette Furtado criticized the acknowledgement of history without any concrete action. One big issue with that 2022 Cameron Center parking lot sleepover was that too many rules were required, such as pre-registration, car insurance, car paperwork, driver's licenses, and people had to vacate very early in the morning. Additionally, there was no food available or bathrooms.

stories.text: What's the Deal with Mixed-Use Development? Aloha, everybody. I'm Senator Angus McKelvey. What is mixed use? If you've been following us for a little while, you know I'm a big fan of mixed use. What it means in layman's terms is integrated residential, commercial, and community spaces. It's the way our towns were designed from very back in the day when they were plantation towns. So many families had their businesses downstairs from where they lived and it provides a real way for us to tackle our housing woes, create more economic opportunity and relieve challenges for businesses who are just as much struggling on trying to get employees. It reduces traffic congestion because now people can truly walk and bike, live and play where they work in their town. It enhances resiliency of our communities. It improves walkability and livability in them and it utilizes infrastructure more efficiently. We can utilize areas that not only have infrastructure but many of these The buildings are already permitted. They have all the necessary approvals. And with these modifications, we can bring housing on now, as opposed to years and years and years as it comes with trying to develop anything from scratch. So, mixed use development, which we are pursuing this year in a bill to create a working group that would have Maui people look at potential opportunities within our own community where the state can partner Aloha, everybody. I'm Senator Angus McKelvey. Stay tuned this legislative session. We need your input on the bills and issues. Mahalo again and have a good week. And that is mixed use.

stories.headline: UH study links food insecurity to poor mental health
stories.summary: A University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa study of 2,270 adults found food insecurity was a major predictor of depression, low self-esteem and suicidal thoughts.
stories.text: A University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa study found that food insecurity is a key driver of poor mental health in Hawaiʻi. Published in the journal Frontiers in Public Health, the study Researchers analyzed 2022 data from 2,270 adults. Nearly 40% reported depression, 15% had low self-esteem, and 4.2% experienced suicidal thoughts. Food insecurity was a major predictor, especially for those with pre-existing health conditions. Researchers emphasize that addressing food insecurity is crucial for mental well-being and community resilience.
